canonical_rules.predicate_text: Synoptic/checklist reporting superior to traditional narrative (free text) reporting for cancer resection specimens
canonical_rules.representative_verbatim: The surgical pathology report on cancer resection specimens is fundamental to providing clinicians with the information needed for adequate patient oncology treatment. Since the multi-institutional quality study on pathology reporting of colorectal cancer published by Zarbo in 1992, many other studies have shown that the use of checklists or synoptic reporting is superior to traditional narrative (free text) reporting. Using electronic health records, synoptic histopathology reporting tools can be designed to be very sophisticated with discrete data fields, drop down menus, and automated SNOMED encoding. The use of discrete data fields ('atomic data') means that it is possible to automatically search, extract, and transmit data electronically. Despite the apparent benefits of electronic synoptic histopathology reporting, and the successful regional implementation of such a reporting system in Ontario, Canada, others have reported that the implementation and use of electronic histopathology reporting is no easy organisational task. Similar challenges have also been reported regarding the implementation and use of a web-based synoptic reporting tool for cancer surgery. From a management and organisational perspective, the list of possible causes for project failure with respect to information technology development, implementation and use is long. In our opinion, a pro-active understanding and management of key organisational issues is a requirement for successful long-term synoptic histopathology cancer reporting.

map_chunks.summary_text: This chunk (PMC4035753) introduces the context for electronic synoptic histopathology reporting in oncology. Synoptic/checklist-based reporting has been shown by multiple studies to be superior to traditional narrative reporting for cancer resection specimens [S2]. Electronic synoptic tools leverage discrete 'atomic' data fields, drop-down menus, and automated SNOMED encoding [S3], which enable automatic data search, extraction, and electronic transmission [S4]. While regional implementation in Ontario, Canada has demonstrated success [S5], multiple reports highlight that implementing and maintaining electronic histopathology reporting and web-based synoptic tools for cancer surgery is a significant organisational challenge [S5, S6]. The authors argue that proactive management of organisational issues is essential for sustained success [S8].

This chunk discusses organisational and stakeholder considerations for transitioning from narrative to synoptic histopathology reporting. All sentences are either administrative/organisational narrative, author/institutional boilerplate, or generic implementation commentary. No generalizable atomic medical facts (morphology, IHC, molecular genetics, staging, treatment, prognosis, or demographic findings) are present. The only clinically adjacent observation — that implementation of a web-based synoptic reporting tool was affected by multilevel organisational factors (S9–S10) — is a healthcare-informatics/implementation science statement, not a histopathological medical fact extractable under the defined categories.

This chunk (PMC4035753_pthy-46-165, sentences S1–S4) describes organisational and user-level factors influencing adoption of synoptic pathology reporting in US pathology departments. Key observations include: asymmetric cost-benefit distribution between laboratories and cancer registries as a barrier to implementation; and wide variability in uptake even when the tool was cost-free, ranging from >90% user rates to zero implementation. These are implementation-science/health-systems observations rather than generalizable histopathological or clinical medical facts, and no extractable atomic clinical findings (morphology, IHC, molecular genetics, staging, treatment, prognosis, or demographic) are present.
